title: Older Adults’ Preferences for Feedback Cadence from an Exercise Coach Robot
extended_summary:
This paper examines how older adults perceive different cadences of feedback from a robot exercise coach. The authors focus on whether changing the frequency of verbal and nonverbal feedback changes perceived usefulness, clarity, timeliness, and helpfulness of the feedback, rather than measuring exercise performance or behavioral change.

The intervention studied is a robot coach that evaluates bicep curls and lateral raises and provides multimodal feedback through speech, facial expressions, and body movements. The study manipulates the cadence of verbal feedback and nonverbal feedback across six conditions, using prerecorded videos of the robot interacting with an exerciser. The design is intended to isolate preferences for feedback frequency in each modality and how one modality influences perceptions of the other.

The population is 100 adults aged 60+ recruited online through Prolific, so the context is an online video-based user study rather than an in-person coaching trial. Participants watched randomized videos and rated the robot’s feedback on Likert scales. The main finding is that medium or high verbal feedback is generally preferred over low verbal feedback, and medium nonverbal feedback is preferred over low nonverbal feedback. The paper also reports cross-modal effects: altering the cadence of one modality changes perceptions of the other modality as well. The authors conclude that feedback cadence should be tuned to older adults’ preferences, while noting that the results are based on viewing videos of another person and may not generalize to being coached directly.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: A generic AI/robot coach system that evaluates user performance and provides verbal and nonverbal feedback with adjustable cadence.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper studies an exercise coach robot that gives verbal and nonverbal feedback at different cadences; participants viewed videos of the robot and rated the feedback.

findings.finding_summary: In an online study of older adults (n=100), changing the cadence of verbal feedback affected perceived clarity and helpfulness of the robot’s verbal feedback. Participants preferred medium and high verbal cadence over low cadence for helpfulness, and high over medium for clarity; no effects on actual exercise performance were measured.
findings.measure: 5-point Likert ratings of verbal feedback clarity and helpfulness after viewing robot exercise-coach videos

findings.finding_summary: Changing the cadence of nonverbal feedback affected perceived timeliness and helpfulness of the robot’s nonverbal feedback. Participants preferred medium nonverbal cadence over low cadence for both measures; the study reports repeated-measures ANOVA significance values but no standardized effect sizes.
findings.measure: 5-point Likert ratings of nonverbal feedback timeliness and helpfulness after viewing robot exercise-coach videos

findings.finding_summary: The cadence of verbal feedback also influenced perceptions of nonverbal feedback: medium and high verbal cadence were associated with better perceived clarity and timeliness of nonverbal feedback than low cadence. This was a perception study only, not a comparison of learning or coaching effectiveness on behavior change.
findings.measure: 5-point Likert ratings of nonverbal feedback clarity and timeliness after viewing robot exercise-coach videos

findings.finding_summary: The cadence of nonverbal feedback affected perceptions of verbal feedback timeliness. Participants preferred medium nonverbal cadence when judging verbal feedback timeliness, but the paper does not report a standardized effect size.
findings.measure: 5-point Likert ratings of verbal feedback timeliness after viewing robot exercise-coach videos

quality_tier_rationale: This is an empirical user study with a clear repeated-measures design, but it is not a K-12 instructional coaching or lesson-feedback study and it measures perceptions from videos rather than behavior change. The evidence is therefore methodologically recognizable but only weakly applicable to the requested educational-use case.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports statistically significant preference/perception differences, but no effect sizes and no educational or student-outcome impact. Because the outcomes are subjective ratings rather than behavior change, the practical impact for K-12 coaching is unclear.
